stem: A GenAI developer at a company is building a RAG application that uses Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases to provide accurate responses to user queries about company documents. The documents include PDF files that contain charts, tables, and text. The company stores the documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company stores structured business data in relational databases. The application must handle 50 queries each minute, provide source attribution, and retrieve information from both structured and unstructured data sources. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as a parser to perform multimodal data processing. Implement structured data retrieval to query databases directly.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation provides multimodal parsing capabilities to extract information from charts, tables, and text in PDF documents. Structured data retrieval allows users to directly query relational databases by using natural language. This approach meets the requirement to retrieve information from both structured and unstructured data sources with the least operational overhead by eliminating the need for custom integrations, Lambda functions, or manual data transformations.

options.text: Use Anthropic Claude Sonnet as a parser. Use default chunking settings and implement federated querying across document sources. Implement structured data retrieval to query databases directly.
options.rationale: Claude Sonnet does not provide the same level of multimodal parsing capabilities as Amazon Bedrock Data Automation to extract information from charts and tables that are embedded in PDF documents. Federated querying and structured data retrieval address the requirement to query both unstructured and structured sources. However, the lack of robust multimodal processing does not fully meet the requirement to handle documents that contain charts and tables.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to perform hierarchical chunking. Use AWS Lambda functions to generate custom SQL queries.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service with hierarchical chunking does not address the requirement to process multimodal content such as charts and tables that are in PDF documents. Additionally, a solution that uses Lambda functions to generate custom SQL queries requires more operational overhead than a solution that uses managed structured data retrieval features to enable direct database querying with natural language.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to enable GraphRAG. Use Amazon Neptune Analytics to model entity relationships in unstructured S3 objects. Use AWS Lambda functions to perform semantic chunking during ingestion and to transform relational database data into graph format to integrate with Neptune.
options.rationale: GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics models entity relationships within unstructured content but does not natively support querying structured data in relational databases. This solution requires Lambda functions to perform semantic chunking and to transform relational database data into graph format. This approach requires more operational overhead than a solution that uses built-in structured data retrieval capabilities.

correct_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as a parser to perform multimodal data processing. Implement structured data retrieval to query databases directly.

stem: A company is building a legal research AI assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock with an Anthropic Claude foundation model (FM). The AI assistant must retrieve highly relevant case law documents to augment the FM's responses. The AI assistant must identify semantic relationships between legal concepts, specific legal terminology, and citations. The AI assistant must perform quickly and return precise results. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a default retrieval configuration. Use Amazon Bedrock to perform post-processing of search results to identify semantic similarity in the documents and to produce precise results.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases provide retrieval capabilities. However, this approach has two critical limitations. The post-processing workflow introduces additional latency, which would fail to meet the requirement to perform quickly. Additionally, a default retrieval configuration that performs post-processing would not provide the same level of integration between semantic understanding and precise terminology matching as OpenSearch Service hybrid search with a dedicated reranker model. This approach does not meet the requirement to identify relationships between legal concepts and exact citations.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch service to deploy a hybrid search architecture that combines vector search with keyword search. Apply an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to optimize result relevance.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service hybrid search combines vector search to identify semantic relationships between legal concepts with keyword search to precisely match specific legal terminology and citations. The Amazon Bedrock reranker model re-scores combined results to optimize relevance and ensure that the most pertinent documents are retrieved quickly. This approach meets all requirements for semantic understanding, precision, and performance.

options.text: Configure an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to use a default vector search configuration. Use Amazon Bedrock to expand queries to improve retrieval for legal documents based on specific terminology and citations.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases support both vector search for semantic understanding of legal concepts and hybrid search that combines vector and keyword search. However, a solution that relies only on default vector search without using a reranker model would fail to optimize for relevance and would not ensure that the most pertinent documents are retrieved quickly.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service with vector search and Amazon Bedrock Titan embeddings to index and search legal documents. Use custom AWS Lambda functions to merge results with keyword-based filters that are stored in an Amazon RDS database.
options.rationale: A solution that uses separate systems to perform vector search and keyword filtering by using custom Lambda functions to merge results would introduce unnecessary architectural complexity and additional latency compared to a solution that uses OpenSearch Service native hybrid search capabilities. This approach fails to meet the requirement to perform quickly and is less efficient than using a dedicated Amazon Bedrock reranker model.

correct_text: Use Amazon OpenSearch service to deploy a hybrid search architecture that combines vector search with keyword search. Apply an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to optimize result relevance.

stem: A GenAI developer at a company is building a customer support analytics platform on Amazon Bedrock. The platform ingests multi-hour transcripts from live support calls and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate summaries, detect sentiment, and recommend next steps. During testing, the GenAI developer notices that long transcripts are being truncated, which causes incomplete responses and missed insights. The GenAI developer needs a solution to ensure that long transcripts are fully processed from beginning to end. The solution must minimize truncation-related errors. The solution must provide high integration reliability across multiple FM calls. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Re-architect the platform to use a larger FM variant that supports extended context windows. Configure truncation diagnostics and adaptive monitoring pipelines.
options.rationale: This solution uses a larger FM that has an extended context window to reduce truncation. However, multi‑hour transcripts exceed even the largest available context windows. Truncation could still occur with this approach, and this solution would not guarantee complete processing for long transcripts. Additionally, larger FMs increase cost and latency, which would not meet the requirement to minimize truncation‑related errors while providing high reliability.

options.text: Implement dynamic chunking strategies to split transcripts into coherent segments. Design prompts to maintain continuity across FM calls and to prioritize lower latency by limiting overlap and by using streamlined overflow detection.
options.rationale: Dynamic chunking divides transcripts into segments to fit within context windows. However, a solution that prioritizes lower latency by limiting overlap can create context gaps at segment boundaries. This approach would not meet the requirement to ensure that transcripts are fully processed from beginning to end. This approach could compromise integration reliability across multiple FM calls.

options.text: Implement dynamic chunking strategies to split transcripts into coherent segments. Design prompts to maintain continuity across segments. Apply diagnostics to detect truncation overflow.
options.rationale: Dynamic chunking strategies divide long transcripts into manageable segments that fit within FM context windows. This approach directly addresses truncation. A solution that designs prompts that maintain continuity across segments and applies diagnostics to detect truncation overflow ensures that long transcripts are fully processed from beginning to end and provides high integration reliability across multiple FM calls.

options.text: Set up semantic summarization and token reduction layers in the platform at a stage before agents send requests to the FM. Configure validation workflows to ensure fidelity of compressed transcripts.
options.rationale: A solution that implements semantic summarization and token‑reduction layers would compress the transcripts before sending them to the FM. However, compression inherently removes details, which would not meet the requirement to ensure full processing of long transcripts without losing insights. This approach would increase the risk of missing important information and would not minimize truncation‑related errors.

correct_text: Implement dynamic chunking strategies to split transcripts into coherent segments. Design prompts to maintain continuity across segments. Apply diagnostics to detect truncation overflow.

stem: A medical company is creating a generative AI (GenAI) system by using Amazon Bedrock. The system processes data from various sources and must maintain end-to-end data lineage. The system must also use real-time personally identifiable information (PII) filtering and audit trails to automatically report compliance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register all data sources and track lineage. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PII filters. Enable AWS CloudTrail logging for all Amazon Bedrock API calls with Amazon S3 integration. Use Amazon Macie to scan stored data for sensitive information and publish findings to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the findings and generate automated compliance reports.
options.rationale: Glue Data Catalog registers and tracks metadata across all data sources to maintain data end-to-end data lineage. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides real-time PII filtering during AI generation by applying sensitive information filters. CloudTrail can capture complete audit trails of all Amazon Bedrock API calls to generate compliance reports. Macie automates compliance scanning of stored data. CloudWatch dashboards can automatically visualize report findings.

options.text: Configure Amazon Athena to query data sources to analyze and report on data lineage. Use Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics to monitor PII exposure in Amazon Bedrock responses and establish OpenTelemetry-based tracing to generate an audit trail. Use an Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels model to detect sensitive information in the data that Amazon Bedrock processes.
options.rationale: Athena queries data but does not maintain lineage relationships between data sources as required. OpenTelemetry-based tracing captures request paths and performance data but does not provide the complete compliance audit trail with automatic reporting required in this scenario. Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels analyzes images but does not filter text-based PII in real-time AI outputs.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to replicate data sources to track lineage. Configure Amazon Macie to scan Amazon Bedrock outputs for sensitive information. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to log user interactions. Deploy Amazon Textract with AWS Step Functions workflows to identify and redact PII from generated reports.
options.rationale: DataSync replicates data between storage locations but does not track data lineage as required. Systems Manager Session Manager logs shell sessions, not API interactions for audit trails. Amazon Textract and Step Functions can extract text from documents post-generation. However, this approach would not provide real-time PII filtering during the generation process.

options.text: Use AWS Config to track data source configurations and changes. Use AWS WAF with custom rules to filter PII at the application layer before Amazon Bedrock processes the data. Configure Amazon EventBridge to capture and route audit events to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical with scheduled AWS Lambda functions to analyze stored outputs for compliance violations.
options.rationale: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes, not data lineage between sources as required. AWS WAF filters web requests at the application layer before processing. It does not filter AI-generated content. Amazon Comprehend Medical and scheduled Lambda functions would provide batch processing rather than real-time PII filtering during generation.

correct_text: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register all data sources and track lineage. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PII filters. Enable AWS CloudTrail logging for all Amazon Bedrock API calls with Amazon S3 integration. Use Amazon Macie to scan stored data for sensitive information and publish findings to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the findings and generate automated compliance reports.

stem: A financial services company is building a fraud detection system by using Amazon Bedrock. The system will monitor activity in multiple stock trading applications that run in the United States and Europe. The system must process 1,000 transactions every second with sub-500 ms response times. The system must also maintain high availability during connectivity disruptions. The company must ensure that data for European customers is processed only in AWS Regions that are based in Europe. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure all applications to use the InvokeModel API with provisioned throughput for an Anthropic Claude model in each Region separately. Set up a custom Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic based on Regional capacity and response times. Implement a Regional failover mechanism that uses Amazon EventBridge rules to handle connectivity disruptions.
options.rationale: Provisioned throughput would provide dedicated capacity to achieve consistent performance. However, this approach lacks the automated cross-Region failover capabilities required to maintain high availability during connectivity disruptions. This solution uses EventBridge rules to handle Regional failover. However, this implementation routes requests only within the same Region without cross-Region inference profiles, which would be required to dynamically route traffic during disruptions.

options.text: Configure applications that run in the United States to use provisioned throughput with the InvokeModel API. Configure European applications to use a Europe-specific geographic inference profile to ensure data sovereignty. Configure automatic scaling for provisioned capacity based on utilization metrics. Use Amazon EventBridge and AWS Lambda functions to implement cross-Region failover mechanisms.
options.rationale: A solution that uses provisioned throughput with the InvokeModel API to support US applications ensures consistent performance to meet the requirement to process 1,000 transactions each second with sub-500 ms response times. Europe-specific geographic inference profiles ensure that data for customers in Europe is processed only within Europe-based Regions. Automatic scaling based on utilization metrics and cross-Region failover that is managed by EventBridge rules and Lambda functions meet the high availability requirement during connectivity disruptions.

options.text: Configure all applications to use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API with on-demand throughput. Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API with Regional endpoints in each location where the company operates to route requests to the closest Amazon Bedrock endpoint. Create separate IAM roles for applications that run in the United States and Europe. Grant the IAM roles Region-specific permissions.
options.rationale: On-demand throughput could experience variable performance and potential throttling at peak loads. This approach would make it difficult to consistently guarantee the sub-500 ms response times required to process 1,000 transactions each second. Additionally, IAM role-based Regional permissions would not provide the same level of automated data sovereignty enforcement as Europe-specific geographic inference profiles.

options.text: Configure AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EKS applications to use the InvokeModel API with a global inference profile. Deploy an automated failover system that uses Amazon Route 53 health checks. Create a dedicated European inference profile and enable Geographic cross-Region inference for European applications. Use Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor utilization metrics.
options.rationale: Global inference profiles route requests to any Region around the world based on availability and performance. This approach would not meet the requirement to process data for European customers only in Europe-based Regions.

correct_text: Configure applications that run in the United States to use provisioned throughput with the InvokeModel API. Configure European applications to use a Europe-specific geographic inference profile to ensure data sovereignty. Configure automatic scaling for provisioned capacity based on utilization metrics. Use Amazon EventBridge and AWS Lambda functions to implement cross-Region failover mechanisms.

stem: A company implements a customer service GenAI application that uses Amazon Bedrock to respond to regulatory compliance questions. The application uses multiple data sources including regulatory documents that are stored in Amazon S3, customer interaction histories, and product documentation. The company needs to implement traceability features that give auditors the ability to verify which specific data sources contribute to each application response. The traceability features must not negatively affect the application's performance at an enterprise scale. The solution must generate decision citations in real time and store citation logs for audits. The solution must handle document updates without requiring the company to redeploy the application. The solution must maintain citation accuracy even when source documents are modified or archived. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with the RetrieveAndGenerate API to enable citations in responses. Configure the application to generate citations that include document sources and metadata. Implement session tracking by using session IDs to maintain conversation context.
options.rationale: This approach provides built-in citation capabilities that automatically include source document references and metadata with each response. This native integration meets the traceability requirement by generating decision citations in real time, handles document updates automatically by using managed indexing to maintain citation accuracy when source documents are modified or archived, and minimizes operational overhead by using fully managed services that do not require custom development or middleware.

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions to intercept each application request and manually track which data sources the application accesses. Store the tracking data in Amazon DynamoDB. Update records whenever the application generates a response.
options.rationale: A solution that uses Lambda functions as middleware to intercept requests and manually track data sources would require extensive custom development and would add latency to each request. This approach would significantly increase operational overhead. This approach lacks built-in capabilities to generate real-time citations and document metadata and would not automatically handle document updates or maintain citation accuracy when source documents are modified or archived.

options.text: Create a custom tracking system in Amazon RDS to record relationships between inputs and outputs. Implement middleware that logs all data that the application accesses during response generation. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to train a model to predict which data influenced each response.
options.rationale: A solution that builds a custom tracking system that uses Amazon RDS and middleware to log data access would require significant operational overhead. A solution that uses SageMaker AI to train a model to predict which data influenced responses would rely on inference rather than actual source tracing. This approach would fail to provide the verifiable traceability required and would not automatically handle document updates to maintain citation accuracy.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails that enforce I/O filtering. Set up detailed logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create custom parsing scripts to extract source attribution information from model responses. Store the parsed data in Amazon S3 for audit purposes.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock guardrails are designed to filter content and enforce safety controls rather than track source attributions as required. A solution that uses custom parsing scripts to extract source attribution would require significant operational overhead. This approach lacks the real-time citation generation and automatic handling for document updates required to maintain citation accuracy when source documents are modified or archived.

correct_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with the RetrieveAndGenerate API to enable citations in responses. Configure the application to generate citations that include document sources and metadata. Implement session tracking by using session IDs to maintain conversation context.

stem: A hospital runs a GenAI application that generates medical reports based on patient bloodwork data. The application uses an Amazon Nova Pro model to generate the reports. Requests for report generation peak during regular work hours. The hospital needs to optimize costs for the application. The hospital also wants to scale the application to meet the demand for multiple hospital departments. The solution must maintain the same level of report quality. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch to log model invocations. Store responses from Nova Pro in Amazon S3. Use the stored responses to create distillation job for a Llama 70B model on Amazon Bedrock. Deploy the Llama model on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
options.rationale: Model distillation in Amazon Bedrock transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller, faster, most cost-effective student model within the same family. However, this approach uses SageMaker JumpStart to deploy the Llama 70B model, which would not optimize costs for the variable demand pattern that peaks during work hours. SageMaker JumpStart requires infrastructure management and does not provide the same cost optimization as on-demand inference for fluctuating workloads.

options.text: Create a training dataset in JSONL that includes medical data and reports written by the hospital staff. Upload the dataset to an Amazon S3 bucket. Include a few examples from the dataset in each prompt to invoke the Nova Pro model.
options.rationale: Few-shot learning adds examples to prompts to improve response quality but does not optimize costs. This approach uses the same Nova Pro model and increases the number of tokens in each prompt by adding examples. This approach would increase inference costs rather than reduce costs.

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch to log model invocations. Store the responses from Nova Pro in Amazon S3. Use the stored responses to create a distillation job for Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock. Deploy Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock and enable on-demand inference.
options.rationale: Model distillation in Amazon Bedrock transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller, faster, most cost-effective student model within the same family. This approach logs invocations from the Nova Pro teacher model, creates a distillation job to train Nova Lite, and deploys with on-demand inference to handle variable demand. This approach meets the requirements to optimize costs, scale for multiple departments, and maintain report quality.

options.text: Create a training dataset in JSONL that includes medical data and reports written by the hospital staff. Upload the dataset to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the training dataset to fine-tune the Nova Pro model. Deploy the fine-tuned model with provisioned throughput on Amazon Bedrock.
options.rationale: Fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock can improve model performance on specific tasks by training the model on labeled data but does not optimize costs. This solution fine-tunes the same Nova Pro model and deploys it with provisioned throughput. This approach would require purchasing fixed capacity and would not reduce inference costs compared to a solution that uses a smaller distilled model to meet the variable demand pattern.

correct_text: Use Amazon CloudWatch to log model invocations. Store the responses from Nova Pro in Amazon S3. Use the stored responses to create a distillation job for Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock. Deploy Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock and enable on-demand inference.

stem: A healthcare company is building a GenAI solution that uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize medical records. The solution must detect and remove protected health information (PHI) from the records. However, the solution must accurately use and summarize medical terminology in the summaries. The company wants to compare multiple foundation models (FMs) to identify the FM that provides the most consistent results. The company wants to test and finalize the build of the solution within 3 weeks. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Build a processing pipeline that uses Amazon Comprehend Medical to identify PHI. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to develop a custom summarization model. Perform manual sampling to assess output quality.
options.rationale: Amazon Comprehend Medical can detect PHI in clinical text. However, a solution that requires building a custom summarization model in SageMaker AI would require significantly more development time than is available on the 3-week timeline. Additionally, this approach does not provide automated comparison across multiple FM to identify the FM that provides the most consistent results.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock to test multiple FMs against sample medical records. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to detect PHI in the generated summaries. Store evaluation results in Amazon DynamoDB. Build custom scoring logic in AWS Lambda to compare medical terminology accuracy across models.
options.rationale: This approach detects PHI reactively after generation by using Amazon Comprehend Medical instead of preventing PHI during generation. This approach does not meet the requirement to remove PHI from records. This approach requires development of custom Lambda scoring logic and involves managing DynamoDB to store evaluation results. This approach requires significant development overhead compared to Amazon Bedrock Evaluations automated model comparison.

options.text: Test prompts against multiple FMs in the Amazon Bedrock console playground. Use manual reviews to assess PHI handling and medical terminology accuracy across sample outputs.
options.rationale: The Amazon Bedrock console playground allows you to test prompts and explore FMs. However, an approach that uses manual reviews would not provide the automated model comparison needed to systematically evaluate multiple FMs against medical terminology accuracy and PHI handling requirements within the 3-week timeline.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply sensitive information filters to detect and mask PHI. Use Amazon Bedrock Evaluations to automatically score outputs against a medical terminology dataset to compare multiple FMs.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides sensitive information filters that can block or mask PHI during generation. This approach meets the requirement to detect and remove PHI from the records. Amazon Bedrock Evaluations can perform automated model comparison by scoring outputs against a domain-specific dataset such as medical terminology. This approach can help select an accurate model within the 3-week timeline.

correct_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply sensitive information filters to detect and mask PHI. Use Amazon Bedrock Evaluations to automatically score outputs against a medical terminology dataset to compare multiple FMs.

stem: A hospital is building an AI application to help medical clinicians to make treatment decisions. The application uses Amazon Bedrock to analyze patient case histories and suggest diagnoses. The application must maintain sub-500 ms response times to integrate with the hospital's existing real-time clinical workflow. To comply with privacy regulations, the application must log all personally identifiable information (PII) handling decisions for audits. The application must detect and remove PII from responses with at least 99% accuracy. After initial deployment, clinicians report that diagnostic summaries from the application occasionally include patient names and medical record numbers that were not present in the original case history inputs. An investigation reveals that Amazon Comprehend Medical successfully detects and removes PII from inputs with 95% accuracy, and the application replaces all detected entities with tokens before it sends inputs to Amazon Bedrock. However, the application continues to generate patient-identifying information in approximately 3-5% of outputs. The company needs a solution to prevent the application from displaying PII in outputs while meeting all other operational requirements. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Remove detailed medical context from case histories during pre-processing to prevent the model from generating patient-specific information based on clinical pattern associations.
options.rationale: A solution that removes detailed medical context would undermine the application's purpose of analyzing patient case histories to suggest diagnoses. This approach incorrectly assumes that reducing medical detail would prevent the model from generating PII. Foundation models can hallucinate patient identifiers even with minimal context based on learned patterns from training data. This solution reduces the usefulness of the application without meeting the requirement to detect and remove PII from responses with at least 99% accuracy.

options.text: Enable session isolation in Amazon Bedrock API calls. Clear conversation history between requests to prevent patient information from persisting across multiple case analyses.
options.rationale: A solution that implements session isolation would address cross-session data leakage but would not prevent the model from generating PII during each session. The application generates PII in 3-5% of outputs because the foundation model generates new identifiers within single inference responses based on training patterns, not because of session state carryover. This solution does not meet the requirement to prevent the application from displaying PII in outputs.

options.text: Implement a secondary PII detection layer by using regular expressions and custom entity recognition to detect identifiers that Amazon Comprehend Medical misses before sending inputs to Amazon Bedrock.
options.rationale: A solution that only improves input PII detection would not prevent hallucinated identifiers from appearing in model outputs. The scenario states that some patient names and medical record numbers that appear in outputs were not present in the original inputs. This indicates that the model is generating new identifiers rather than leaking existing ones from inputs. Secondary input filtering layers would address identifiers that are already present in case histories and would fail to meet the requirement to prevent the application from displaying PII in outputs.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with sensitive information filters to detect and block PII in model outputs.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock guardrails can apply sensitive information filters to detect and block or mask PII in model outputs before they reach the application. Foundation models can hallucinate realistic-sounding patient identifiers based on training patterns, even when those identifiers are not within inputs. A solution that configures guardrails to apply PII output filters addresses the requirement to prevent PII from displaying in outputs while maintaining sub-500 ms response times and providing the required audit logging.

correct_text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails with sensitive information filters to detect and block PII in model outputs.

stem: A financial services company runs an AI application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs) to generate personalized investment recommendations based on customer documents. The AI application processes customer portfolios, financial statements, and regulatory documentation to create personalized recommendations. The company is experiencing inconsistent model performance because of poor data quality. Some documents contain personally identifiable information (PII) that the company must redact. Other documents contain formatting inconsistencies that confuse the FMs. The company needs a solution that ensures consistent, high-quality inputs to optimize FM. The solution must comply with financial regulations and PII handling policies. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie to automatically detect and redact PII. Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon Textract to enforce standard document formatting. Create dynamic prompts that adapt to individual document schemas to improve model consistency.
options.rationale: Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in Amazon S3 by running automated discovery jobs and scheduled scans. However, Macie does not provide document pre-processing capabilities for FMs. This solution requires custom Lambda functions to format the documents and does not address the formatting inconsistencies that confuse FMs. This approach requires more operational overhead compared to a solution that uses managed document analysis services that directly improve FM input quality.

options.text: Use Amazon Textract to analyze document structures and extract text. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII and analyze sentiment. Design prompt engineering strategies that use structured metadata to improve FM reasoning and reduce hallucinations.
options.rationale: Amazon Textract analyzes document structures and converts unstructured documents into structured, machine-readable formats with metadata about tables, forms, and key-value pairs. This approach directly addresses the formatting inconsistencies that confuse the FMs. Amazon Comprehend provides managed PII detection and redaction for document pre-processing pipelines, which ensures compliance with PII handling policies. This approach uses structured metadata from Amazon Textract in prompt engineering strategies to improve FM reasoning and reduce hallucinations, which meets the requirement to provide consistent, high-quality inputs with the least operational overhead.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter out PII during inference. Use pre-processing AWS Lambda functions to standardized document formatting. Use few-shot prompting techniques and standardized examples to improve model performance across document types.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock guardrails filter content during or after inference to prevent harmful outputs. However, guardrails would not address the poor data quality or formatting inconsistencies in the input documents. The root cause of inconsistent model performance is the unstructured and inconsistent input data that confuses the FMs.

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII by using custom entity recognition. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate document preprocessing workflows. Use prompt templates with conditional logic to handle schema variations effectively.
options.rationale: Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition requires you to train custom models and manage additional machine learning (ML) workflows. This approach would require more operational overhead than necessary to perform standard PII detection. This solution uses Step Functions to orchestrate pre-processing workflows and conditional logic in prompt templates. This approach would be more complex than a solution that uses managed services.

correct_text: Use Amazon Textract to analyze document structures and extract text. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII and analyze sentiment. Design prompt engineering strategies that use structured metadata to improve FM reasoning and reduce hallucinations.

stem: A financial services company is developing a GenAI document-processing application that multiple business units will use. The application must support both Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FM) and models that are hosted in Amazon SageMaker AI. The company must have consistent security controls across development and production environments. The company wants a solution that provides comprehensive monitoring, logging, and observability. The company wants to build the application by using reusable approved technical components that are shared across business units. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Develop a standardized AWS CDK construct library that implements consistent prompt management, security controls, and observability components. Package the constructs as a shared library that all business units will use.
options.rationale: AWS CDK constructs are reusable building blocks that consolidate infrastructure, configuration, and application logic into standardized components. A shared CDK construct library would allow the company to enforce consistent prompt management, security controls, and observability across all business units while supporting both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI models. This approach meets the requirement to provide reusable, approved components and consistent cross-environment governance.

options.text: Create a separate AWS CloudFormation template for each business unit. Customize deployments by using parameters for environment-specific configurations.
options.rationale: CloudFormation is an infrastructure as code (IaC) service that gives you the ability to model and provision AWS resources consistently across environments. However, a solution that creates separate templates for each business unit would not ensure standardized, reusable components or consistent security controls. This approach would lead to template drift, duplicated effort, and inconsistent implementations.

options.text: Deploy all GenAI workloads into a single AWS account that uses a multi-tenant architecture. Configure separate IAM policies and resource-based permissions for each business unit.
options.rationale: Multi-tenant architectures can isolate workloads by using AWS IAM and resource policies. However, a solution that places all GenAI workloads in a single AWS account would increase the blast radius. This approach does not provide the required governance model. This approach does not deliver reusable shared components, and it does not ensure consistent security controls across development and production environments for multiple business units.

options.text: Build a custom SageMaker AI pipeline for each business unit. Set up a separate inference endpoint for each pipeline. Use AWS Step Functions to coordinate model inference requests. Implement custom monitoring solutions for each deployment.
options.rationale: SageMaker AI pipelines automate ML workflows such as training, tuning, and deployment. A solution that builds a separate custom pipeline for each business unit would create fragmentation, inconsistent security controls, and duplicated monitoring solutions. This approach does not meet the requirement to provide shared, reusable components and unified observability across environments.

correct_text: Develop a standardized AWS CDK construct library that implements consistent prompt management, security controls, and observability components. Package the constructs as a shared library that all business units will use.

stem: A financial services company is developing a GenAI application that needs to analyze data across multiple AWS accounts by using a foundation model (FM). The data and application are in Amazon S3 buckets in three separate accounts. Account A contains transaction data. Account B contains customer profiles, including personally identifiable information (PII). Account C hosts the GenAI application. The company plans to add data sources from seven more business units within the next few months. The company must have strict control over PII data. The company must ensure that the FM accesses only necessary data fields. The company needs a solution to establish secure cross-account access for the GenAI application. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS IAM Identity Center to create a permission set for the FM service account. Configure resource-based policies on each S3 bucket to allow specific access to Account C. Deploy a custom AWS Lambda authorizer to filter PII data before passing it to the FM.
options.rationale: IAM Identity Center manages single sign-on and user access across AWS accounts and applications. IAM Identity Center does not provide column-level access control for data. Lambda authorizers are designed to handle API request authorization and do not provide granular field-level control over PII data across S3 buckets in multiple accounts.

options.text: Configure resource-based policies on S3 buckets in each source account to allow access from the GenAI application in Account C. Configure identity-based policies for the FM's service role that allow access only to specific data columns by using AWS Lake Formation tag-based access controls. Set up a VPC endpoint in each account to provide secure cross-account access.
options.rationale: A solution that uses Lake Formation tag-based access control would require you to register the S3 buckets with Lake Formation and grant permissions through Lake Formation permissions APIs. You cannot implement Lake Formation tag-based access control by using resource-based policies on S3 buckets alone. Additionally, VPC endpoints provide network-level isolation but do not enable the cross-account access and column-level data filtering required to ensure that the FM accesses only necessary data fields.

options.text: Set up AWS Lake Formation in each source account. Register the S3 buckets with Lake Formation. Create IAM roles in each source account that have permissions to access specific S3 bucket paths. Configure Lake Formation permissions to allow access only to specific data columns by using Lake Formation tag-based access controls. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to deploy the FM with an execution role in Account C that can assume the cross-account IAM roles to access the data through Lake Formation.
options.rationale: Lake Formation provides column-level access control through tag-based access controls. This approach gives you the ability to ensure that the FM accesses only necessary data fields. Lake Formation registers S3 buckets in each source account and enables secure cross-account data sharing through IAM roles. SageMaker AI can deploy the FM with an execution role that assumes the cross-account roles to access data through Lake Formation. This approach meets the requirements to enforce strict PII control and provide scalability to 10 total accounts.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock cross-account IAM roles. Create role-based access policies in each source account that allow access only for specific S3 bucket paths. Apply tag-based access controls on S3 objects to classify and control access to PII data.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock cross-account IAM roles can enable cross-account access. However, S3 tag-based access controls operate at the object level and cannot restrict access to specific columns or fields within data objects. This approach does not meet the requirement to ensure that the FM accesses only necessary data fields.

correct_text: Set up AWS Lake Formation in each source account. Register the S3 buckets with Lake Formation. Create IAM roles in each source account that have permissions to access specific S3 bucket paths. Configure Lake Formation permissions to allow access only to specific data columns by using Lake Formation tag-based access controls. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to deploy the FM with an execution role in Account C that can assume the cross-account IAM roles to access the data through Lake Formation.

stem: A media company needs to automatically generate searchable metadata for a video library that contains 10,000 hours of content. Each video includes visual scenes, spoken dialogue, background music, and on-screen text. The company needs a solution to extract scene descriptions, speaker transcripts with timestamps, text overlay content, and emotional context from each video. The output must synchronize all metadata types with one another and create a searchable index. Users must be able to search based on any metadata type and jump directly to a specific moment in each video. What solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon SageMaker AI processing job that extracts video frames at fixed intervals and attaches timestamps. Use Amazon Transcribe with time markers enabled to process audio. Use an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock to analyze frame-transcript pairs. Store outputs in a unified JSON structure that preserves temporal relationships.
options.rationale: SageMaker AI processing jobs orchestrate video frame extraction at fixed intervals with timestamps. Amazon Transcribe automatically provides word-level timestamps to provide timeline alignment in all transcript outputs. Claude models in Amazon Bedrock can analyze frame-transcript pairs to perform multimodal scene analysis, including emotional context. The unified JSON structure preserves temporal relationships, which gives users the ability to search based on any metadata type and jump directly to a specific moment in each video.

options.text: Create an Amazon SageMaker AI processing job that extracts video frames at regular intervals. Use Amazon Transcribe to process audio and perform speech-to-text conversions. Use an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock to process frames individually to produce multimodal scene analyses. Store outputs in separate Amazon S3 buckets that are organized by content type.
options.rationale: SageMaker AI processing jobs can orchestrate video frame extraction. Amazon Transcribe performs speech-to-text conversions. However, a solution that stores outputs in separate S3 buckets that are organized by content type will prevent synchronization of all metadata types with one another as required. Users would not be able to jump directly to a specific moment based on searchable metadata.

options.text: Create an Amazon SageMaker AI processing job that configures Anthropic Claude Opus in Amazon Bedrock to produce a comprehensive multimodal analysis for each video. Configure the processing job to extract metadata by using a single inference request and to index results in Amazon OpenSearch Service to provide temporal search capabilities.
options.rationale: Claude models in Amazon Bedrock support multimodal analysis of text and images but cannot process entire video files directly through a single inference request. Claude models work with individual frames and text, not video streams. A solution that processes an entire video in a single request would exceed payload and token limitations.

options.text: Create an Amazon SageMaker AI parallel processing job that is orchestrated by a SageMaker AI pipeline. Configure multiple steps in the pipeline to extract video segments, process audio streams by using Amazon Transcribe, analyze video frames by using Amazon Rekognition to detect text in scenes, use Amazon Comprehend to perform sentiment analysis, and store unified metadata in Amazon DynamoDB with time-based partitioning.
options.rationale: SageMaker AI parallel processing jobs, Amazon Transcribe, and Amazon Rekognition can extract video segments, process audio streams, and detect text in scenes. However, Amazon Comprehend is a text-only natural language processing service that cannot analyze emotional context from visual scenes, spoken dialogue, or background music.

correct_text: Create an Amazon SageMaker AI processing job that extracts video frames at fixed intervals and attaches timestamps. Use Amazon Transcribe with time markers enabled to process audio. Use an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock to analyze frame-transcript pairs. Store outputs in a unified JSON structure that preserves temporal relationships.

stem: An education company is building a GenAI-powered student advisor application that uses Amazon Bedrock. The application includes a student advisor AI agent that answers general academic questions. When student queries relate to scholarships, internship planning, or mental health resources, the application should delegate to specialized agents. The application must maintain conversation context across all the specialized agents. The company wants to track usage metrics for the specialized agents. The company wants a solution that requires minimal custom code development. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Create a separate agent in Strands Agents for each topic. Expose the agents through Amazon API Gateway. Configure an AWS Lambda function to route questions to the appropriate agent. Store conversation context in Amazon DynamoDB. Use Amazon CloudWatch logs to track metrics from the Lambda function.
options.rationale: This option requires custom infrastructure including API Gateway, Lambda functions, and DynamoDB. This approach would require significant custom code development and operational overhead.

options.text: Create a separate agent in Strands Agents for each topic. Deploy the agents separately in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Build a frontend client that routes questions to the appropriate agent by using keyword matching. Store conversation transcripts in Amazon S3. Use AgentCore logs and frontend analytics to track agent usage metrics.
options.rationale: This solution relies on frontend client keyword matching for routing. This approach would require significant custom development and lacks the dynamic, context-aware delegation provided by a Strands Agents supervisor pattern. This approach would not meet the requirements to minimize custom code development and operational effort.

options.text: Use Strands Agents to configure a supervisor agent. Use AWS Lambda functions to classify student questions and route them to topic-specific agents for scholarships, internships, and mental health resources. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the delegation workflow between the supervisor agent and specialized agents. Track delegations by collecting Lambda function logs in Amazon CloudWatch.
options.rationale: Strands Agents provides native multi-agent orchestration patterns including agents-as-tools, handoffs, swarms, and graphs that handle delegation without custom Lambda functions or Step Functions workflows. However, this approach would require unnecessary custom code development to support classification and routing.

options.text: Use Strands Agents to configure a supervisor agent. Deploy the supervisor agent in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Register specialized agents for scholarships, internships, and mental health resources as agents that the supervisor can delegate to. Use Strands Agents built-in orchestration capabilities to guide delegation. Use AgentCore Observability to track metrics.
options.rationale: Strands Agents provides native multi-agent orchestration patterns including agents-as-tools that enable a main agent to delegate tasks to specialized agents while maintaining conversation context through built-in memory management. AgentCore Runtime provides serverless scaling, session isolation, and integrated observability through AgentCore Observability. This approach meets the requirements to minimize custom code development and operational effort.

correct_text: Use Strands Agents to configure a supervisor agent. Deploy the supervisor agent in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Register specialized agents for scholarships, internships, and mental health resources as agents that the supervisor can delegate to. Use Strands Agents built-in orchestration capabilities to guide delegation. Use AgentCore Observability to track metrics.

stem: A financial services company is developing a natural language processing (NLP) application that uses an AWS Lambda function to process customer trade inquiries by using Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The Lambda function must generate comprehensive trade analysis responses that typically exceed 4 MB and require 15–20 seconds to complete. The application must respond to customer inquiries in less than 10 seconds and comply with financial regulatory requirements to retain records for 10 years. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon SQS queues to implement asynchronous invocations. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor response times.
options.rationale: This approach would place Lambda events in an SQS queue and return immediately without waiting for the function to finish running. This approach would not respond to customer inquiries in less than 10 seconds as required. This approach would require customers to poll for results separately.

options.text: Implement response streaming to display partial responses as the application generates them. Set a 15-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Use Amazon CloudWatch Lambda Insights to monitor performance.
options.rationale: Response streaming allows the Lambda function to return partial responses as the responses are generated, which can help meet the 10-second initial response requirement. However, the 15-second timeout is insufficient for processing that typically requires 15–20 seconds to finish running and would cause the function to be terminated before completion. CloudWatch Lambda Insights provides performance monitoring but does not address the requirement to retain records for 10 years.

options.text: Implement response streaming to display partial responses as the application generates them. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Store complete response records in Amazon S3.
options.rationale: Response streaming allows the Lambda function to return partial responses immediately as the responses are generated, which would help meet the 10-second initial response requirement. The 30-second timeout accommodates the 15–20 second processing time with an appropriate buffer. Amazon S3 provides durable storage that supports the 10-year retention requirement.

options.text: Use Amazon API Gateway to poll the application. Integrate the application with Amazon ElastiCache to cache responses. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Collect detailed Amazon CloudWatch logs for application performance.
options.rationale: Without response streaming, API Gateway must wait for the entire 15–20 second processing time before returning a response. This approach would not meet the requirement to respond to customer inquiries in less than 10 seconds. ElastiCache provides caching for repeated queries but does not address the initial response time requirement or the need to store complete response records for 10 years.

correct_text: Implement response streaming to display partial responses as the application generates them. Set a 30-second timeout for Lambda function execution time. Store complete response records in Amazon S3.

stem: A legal research company is developing an AI-powered chat assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock with a knowledge base that contains millions of legal documents. When attorneys search for legal case precedents, the initial retrieval returns many documents. The company wants the chat assistant to generate all responses within 3 seconds. The foundation model (FM) that the chat assistant uses has a context window limitation that allows effective processing for only 10 documents for each query. Currently, the retrieval configuration fetches 50 documents by using semantic search. Attorneys report that highly relevant precedents frequently appear in positions 15–40 of the results. The company needs a solution to improve the relevance of query results. The solution must meet the company's latency and context window constraints. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Implement a post-processing action group by using an AWS Lambda function that retrieves 50 documents and calculates cosine similarity scores between the query embedding and each document embedding by using Amazon Titan Embeddings. Configure the action group to sort by similarity score and return the top 10 documents.
options.rationale: Cosine similarity between embeddings is already used during the initial semantic search, so a solution that recalculates the same metric in a Lambda function would produce nearly identical rankings and would not improve relevance. Because this approach does not introduce a new ranking signal, it cannot promote relevant documents from positions 15–40 into the top 10 as required by the model’s context window. This approach adds latency without solving the core retrieval quality problem.

options.text: Maintain the 50-document retrieval but increase the FM's temperature parameter. Implement prompt engineering techniques that instruct the model to identify the most relevant documents from the full result set before the model generates responses.
options.rationale: The temperature parameter in an FM controls the randomness of generated text and does not influence how retrieved documents are ranked or selected. Because temperature affects only the style of the model’s output and not the ordering of retrieved documents, temperature cannot elevate relevant documents from positions 15–40 into the top 10 as required by the model’s context window. This approach fails to improve retrieval relevance and does not meet the company’s latency or context constraints.

options.text: Enable reranking on the knowledge base by using a reranker model with language-specific configurations. Configure the chat assistant to initially retrieve 50 documents. Use the reranker model's cross-encoder architecture to evaluate query-document pairs. Return only the top 10 highest-scored documents.
options.rationale: A reranker model in Amazon Bedrock uses a cross-encoder architecture that jointly evaluates a query and each retrieved document to produce a highly accurate relevance score. Because reranking reorders the initial 50 semantic search results and returns only the top 10 most relevant documents, this approach ensures that important precedents that appear in positions 15–40 are promoted into the model’s context window while meeting the 3-second latency requirement. This approach directly improves retrieval quality and aligns with the FM’s 10-document processing limit.

options.text: Configure three separate knowledge bases. Configure one knowledge base to use 500 token chunks, another to use 1,000 token chunks, and the third to use 2,000 token chunks. Implement a pre-processing action group by using an AWS Lambda function that retrieves 50 documents from each knowledge base, merges the 150 total results, and uses term frequency - inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) scoring to select the top 10 documents.
options.rationale: A solution that uses multiple knowledge bases and multiple chunk sizes and merges results by using a Lambda function would introduce unnecessary architectural complexity and increase retrieval latency. Because TF-IDF is a lexical matching technique that does not capture semantic meaning, this approach is far less effective than cross-encoder reranking at identifying legally relevant precedents that are deeper in the result list. This approach is unlikely to meet the 3-second response requirement and would not reliably improve relevance.

correct_text: Enable reranking on the knowledge base by using a reranker model with language-specific configurations. Configure the chat assistant to initially retrieve 50 documents. Use the reranker model's cross-encoder architecture to evaluate query-document pairs. Return only the top 10 highest-scored documents.

stem: A healthcare company is building an AI assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize patient case notes. The company stores the case notes in Amazon S3. The AI assistant must process 20,000 case notes daily with peak loads of 100 requests every minute. The AI assistant must maintain sub-second pre-processing latency. The company must ensure that all personally identifiable information (PII) is removed from notes before any text is sent to Amazon Bedrock. The AI assistant must be able to detect PII in both English and Spanish and prevent the foundation model (FM) from returning medical identifiers in generated summaries. The AI assistant must detect PII and provide audit visibility for all redacted fields. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie to detect PII before invoking the FM. Configure AWS WAF rules to block outbound responses that contain sensitive patient data. Store all processed case notes in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.rationale: Amazon Macie is designed to discover and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3 objects. Macie cannot provide real-time PII detection for each incoming request to an FM. Macie cannot perform redaction with sub-second latency as required to pre-process 100 requests each minute. AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP requests and cannot filter content in FM-generated responses. This approach would not meet the requirements redact PII in multiple languages in real time before invoking the FM.

options.text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to apply a one-time masking transformation to all case notes. Send the masked notes to Amazon Bedrock and implement AWS Lake Formation column-level security to restrict downstream access.
options.rationale: AWS Glue DataBrew performs batch data transformations and cannot provide the continuous, real-time PII detection required to process 20,000 case notes daily with sub-second latency. A one-time masking transformation would not protect new case notes that arrive daily. Lake Formation manages data access permissions but cannot detect PII in case notes or filter medical identifiers from Amazon Bedrock FM outputs as required.

options.text: Implement a multi-stage PII detection workflow that uses Amazon Comprehend to detect standard PII types. Implement a fine-tuned Amazon Bedrock model to detect specialty medical identifiers. Combine outputs to create a redacted version of each note and then invoke Amazon Bedrock to summarize the notes. Store audit logs in Amazon S3 to record redaction decisions.
options.rationale: A multi-stage workflow that includes Amazon Comprehend and a fine-tuned Amazon Bedrock model to detect PII would require unnecessary processing steps that would increase latency. This approach would likely not meet the requirement to provide the sub-second pre-processing latency needed to process 100 requests each minute. Amazon Comprehend built-in PII detection capabilities would meet the requirement to detect PII in both English and Spanish without the need for additional FM fine tuning.

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII in English and Spanish case notes and to apply automatic redaction before the AI assistant invokes Amazon Bedrock. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to block disallowed medical identifiers in model outputs. Store redacted input and output logs in Amazon S3 for auditing.
options.rationale: Amazon Comprehend provides built-in PII detection and redaction capabilities for unstructured text in English and Spanish and can achieve sub-second pre-processing latency for the required 100 requests each minute. Amazon Bedrock guardrails filter prohibited medical identifiers in generated summaries. This approach meets the requirement to prevent the FM from returning sensitive identifiers. This approach stores redacted input and output logs in Amazon S3 to provide audit visibility for all redacted fields as required.

correct_text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII in English and Spanish case notes and to apply automatic redaction before the AI assistant invokes Amazon Bedrock. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to block disallowed medical identifiers in model outputs. Store redacted input and output logs in Amazon S3 for auditing.

stem: A company runs a GenAI application that uses multiple foundation models (FMs) from Amazon Bedrock to generate text. The application serves users across three AWS Regions. The application runs on AWS Lambda functions. The company needs to implement dynamic model selection based on response quality and latency metrics. The company must be able to switch between models without modifying or redeploying the application code. The company wants to gradually roll out new models, starting with 20% of traffic. The company needs a solution that will automatically roll back if error rates exceed 1%. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store model selection configurations in Amazon DynamoDB. Use global tables to enable multi-Region replication. Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to monitor Amazon CloudWatch metrics for errors and invoke AWS Lambda functions that update the DynamoDB table with model preferences. Add custom code to the Lambda functions to query DynamoDB before each model invocation.
options.rationale: This solution requires you to add custom code to the Lambda functions to query DynamoDB before each model invocation. This approach does not meet the requirement to switch models without modifying or redeploying the application code. DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region replication. However, this approach lacks built-in mechanisms to provide controlled gradual rollout starting with exactly 20% of traffic and automatic rollback when error rates exceed 1%.

options.text: Create Lambda function versions for each model configuration. Use Lambda aliases and set up routing configurations to gradually shift traffic between versions, starting with 20% of traffic. Implement AWS CodeDeploy deployments that monitor Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the Lambda function versions to automatically roll back deployments when error rates exceed thresholds.
options.rationale: Lambda aliases with routing configurations can split traffic between function versions, but this approach requires a separate Lambda function version for each model configuration change. This approach requires redeploying code for each model switch, which does not meet the requirement to switch between models without modifying or redeploying the application code.

options.text: Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to monitor response quality and latency metrics. Implement custom logic in the Lambda functions to select models based on metric thresholds. Use environment variables that are stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to define model selection parameters that can be updated across Regions.
options.rationale: This solution uses custom logic within Lambda functions to select models based on metrics. This approach requires code updates whenever model selection logic changes, which does not meet the requirement to switch models without modifying or redeploying application code. Parameter Store can store environment variables that are updated without code redeployment. However, this approach lacks built-in capabilities to control gradual rollout starting with exactly 20% of traffic and automatic rollback when error rates exceed 1%.

options.text: Use AWS AppConfig to create feature flags for model selection criteria. Set up validation rules for error rates. Implement the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension to retrieve model configurations when the functions run. Define linear deployment strategies to gradually release new models, starting with 20% of traffic.
options.rationale: AppConfig provides dynamic configuration management without code deployments by using feature flags and deployment strategies. The AppConfig Agent Lambda extension retrieves configurations at runtime without requiring code changes to switch models. AppConfig supports linear deployment strategies that can gradually roll out changes starting with 20% of traffic. This solution includes built-in validation rules and automatic rollback capabilities based on CloudWatch error metrics when thresholds are exceeded.

correct_text: Use AWS AppConfig to create feature flags for model selection criteria. Set up validation rules for error rates. Implement the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension to retrieve model configurations when the functions run. Define linear deployment strategies to gradually release new models, starting with 20% of traffic.

stem: A company provides a service that helps users from around the world discover new restaurants. The service has 50 million monthly active users. The company wants to implement a semantic search solution across a database that contains 20 million restaurants and 200 million reviews. The company currently stores the data in a PostgreSQL database. The solution must support complex natural language queries and return results for at least 95% of queries within 500 ms. The solution must maintain data freshness for restaurant details that update hourly. The solution must also scale cost-effectively during peak usage periods. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Implement keyword-based search rules that use custom analyzers and relevance tuning to find restaurants based on attributes such as cuisine type, feature, and location. Create Amazon API Gateway HTTP API endpoints to transform user queries into structured search parameters.
options.rationale: Keyword-based search with custom analyzers would not support complex natural language queries. Keyword search relies on exact or partial text matching rather than semantic understanding, which is necessary to interpret the natural language of user queries.

options.text: Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from restaurant descriptions, reviews, and menu items. When users submit natural language queries, convert the queries to embeddings by using the same FM. Perform k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) searches to find semantically similar results.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service with k-NN search enables semantic search by converting natural language queries and restaurant data into vector embeddings by using an Amazon Bedrock FM. This approach supports complex natural language queries and provides sub-500 ms query performance at scale. OpenSearch Service automatically scales to handle peak usage periods cost-effectively. The managed infrastructure minimizes development effort compared to solutions that require custom implementations.

options.text: Store the restaurant data in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and implement a pgvector extension. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from restaurant data. Store the vector embeddings directly in RDS for PostgreSQL. Create an AWS Lambda function to convert natural language queries to vector representations by using the same FM. Configure the Lambda function to perform similarity searches within the database.
options.rationale: RDS for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension supports vector embeddings for semantic search. However, this solution would require significantly more development effort than a solution that uses managed services such as OpenSearch Service. This approach requires a Lambda function to convert natural language queries to vectors at runtime. You would need to manage integrations between Lambda and RDS for PostgreSQL.

options.text: Migrate restaurant data to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base by using a custom ingestion pipeline. Configure the knowledge base to automatically generate embeddings from restaurant information. Use the Amazon Bedrock Retrieve API with built-in vector search capabilities to query the knowledge base directly by using natural language input.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases are designed to support RAG workflows. Knowledge bases do not support direct semantic search at the scale of this scenario. A solution that uses a custom ingestion pipeline to migrate 20 million restaurants and 200 million reviews into a knowledge base would require significantly more development effort compared to a solution that uses OpenSearch Service directly. Knowledge bases also add unnecessary overhead for this use case because only semantic search is needed, not response generation.

correct_text: Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from restaurant descriptions, reviews, and menu items. When users submit natural language queries, convert the queries to embeddings by using the same FM. Perform k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) searches to find semantically similar results.

stem: A global company uses an organization in AWS Organizations to manage 25 AWS accounts. The company is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to build an AI assistant. The AI assistant must access customer data that is stored in multiple AWS accounts across several business units. The AI assistant needs to perform actions on behalf of specific users by querying Amazon DynamoDB tables that contain customer information in each business unit's AWS account. Each business unit maintains its own AWS account that hosts its own DynamoDB tables. The company must enforce strict data access security boundaries. The solution must allow the AI assistant to access resources across multiple accounts while preserving user identity context. The solution must support the company's plan to expand to more than 40 AWS accounts in the next year. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure SCPs for the organization to explicitly allow the AI assistant's execution role principal to perform dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query actions across all member accounts. Configure the AI assistant to reference cross-account DynamoDB table ARNs directly in their resource definitions.
options.rationale: SCPs can only restrict permissions as guardrails. SCPs cannot grant permissions across accounts. SCPs define maximum available permissions but do not enable cross-account resource access for the AgentCore execution role. This approach would fail to meet the requirement for the AI assistant to access DynamoDB tables in business unit accounts.

options.text: Configure the AI assistant to use an outbound credential provider that runs AssumeRole operations to dynamically obtain temporary credentials so the AI assistant can access resources across accounts. Create an IAM role in each business unit account that has a trust relationship to the AI assistant's execution role and permissions to access the DynamoDB tables. Ensure that AssumeRole calls include session tags to identify the end user.
options.rationale: This solution uses an outbound credential provider that runs AssumeRole operations to provide cross-account resource access. This approach uses session tags to preserve user identities. This approach requires the least operational overhead because the AI assistant can scale to more than 40 accounts with minimal configuration changes for each new account.

options.text: Create a separate AI assistant in each business unit account. Deploy an Amazon API Gateway REST API that runs request routing logic. Create AWS Lambda authorizers to direct user queries to the appropriate AI assistant based on the customer's business unit identifier from the request context.
options.rationale: This approach would require unnecessary operational overhead to deploy a separate AI assistant to each business unit account with unique API Gateway routing logic. This approach would also require operational overhead to manage 25 separate AI assistant instances initially. When the company scales to more than 40 instances, this solution would result in duplicated maintenance, updates, and management overhead across all accounts.

options.text: Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the DynamoDB tables from each business unit account to a central account where the AI assistant runs. Configure AWS RAM permissions to allow cross-account access to the DynamoDB tables. Grant the AgentCore execution role permissions to access the shared resources directly.
options.rationale: DynamoDB tables are not a shareable resource type in AWS RAM. AWS RAM supports specific resource types such as VPC subnets, transit gateways, and license manager configurations.

correct_text: Configure the AI assistant to use an outbound credential provider that runs AssumeRole operations to dynamically obtain temporary credentials so the AI assistant can access resources across accounts. Create an IAM role in each business unit account that has a trust relationship to the AI assistant's execution role and permissions to access the DynamoDB tables. Ensure that AssumeRole calls include session tags to identify the end user.
