stem: A media company is building an AI-powered content moderation system by using Amazon Bedrock. The system first classifies text by using a small, low-latency model. Then the system escalates requests that have a confidence score below 0.65 to a larger, more expensive model. The system must respond in near real time for high-confidence results. The system must process low-confidence requests asynchronously. The system must scale to meet sudden spikes in demand. The company wants to optimize costs for the system by invoking the larger model only when required. The company wants to use decoupled components to achieve high resiliency for the system. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an AWS Step Functions workflow that has parallel branches to run both the small model and the large model for every request. Choose the large model result when confidence score values differ.
options.rationale: AWS Step Functions is a serverless orchestration service that coordinates distributed applications and microservices by using visual workflows. However, this approach runs both models in parallel for every request, which does not meet the requirement to optimize costs by invoking the larger model only when necessary. This approach does not provide the decoupled, message-driven architecture needed to scale and handle sudden spikes in demand.

options.text: Deploy both models on Amazon EC2 instances and enable auto scaling. Use a custom application heuristic to route requests to the appropriate instance based on phrase length and keyword rules.
options.rationale: Amazon EC2 provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. A solution that deploys models on EC2 instances with custom heuristic-based routing requires operational overhead to manage infrastructure, provides less reliable routing compared to confidence-based cascading, and does not offer the decoupled, message-driven architecture required to achieve high resiliency and handle sudden spikes in demand.

options.text: Send requests to an Amazon SQS queue. Use AWS Fargate to process messages. Invoke the small model first. If the confidence score is below 0.65, place the request in a second SQS queue to process asynchronously by using the large model.
options.rationale: Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queuing service that decouples and scales distributed systems. Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. A solution that uses SQS queues would provide a resilient buffer that decouples components and absorbs sudden spikes in demand. Fargate can process messages with controlled parallelism. This approach invokes the small model first to provide near real-time responses and then escalates only low-confidence request to a second SQS queue for asynchronous processing by the larger model. This approach meets the cost optimization, resiliency, and latency requirements.

options.text: Use Amazon API Gateway to invoke the small model synchronously. If the small model's confidence score is below 0.65, synchronously call the larger model. Use provisioned concurrency to handle traffic spikes.
options.rationale: API Gateway is a fully managed service that gives you the ability to create, publish, and maintain APIs at any scale. However, this solution does not decouple producers and consumers because API Gateway directly invokes backend services synchronously without providing a buffer for traffic spikes. Additionally, this approach makes synchronous calls to both models when confidence is low, which does not meet the requirement to enable asynchronous processing for low-confidence requests.

correct_text: Send requests to an Amazon SQS queue. Use AWS Fargate to process messages. Invoke the small model first. If the confidence score is below 0.65, place the request in a second SQS queue to process asynchronously by using the large model.

stem: A pharmaceutical company is developing a RAG application that uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The knowledge base uses Amazon OpenSearch Service as a data source for more than 25 million scientific papers. Users report that the application produces inconsistent answers that cite irrelevant sections of papers when queries span methodology, results, and discussion sections of the papers. The company needs to improve the knowledge base to preserve semantic context across related paragraphs on the scale of the entire corpus of data. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the knowledge base to use hierarchical chunking. Use parent chunks that contain 1,000 tokens and child chunks that contain 200 tokens. Set a 50-token overlap between chunks.
options.rationale: This approach organizes data into parent layers of 1,000 tokens and child layers of 200 tokens. In standard knowledge base retrieval, a retrieved child can be replaced by its parent to provide broader context. If a user asks, “How did the cross-validation method affect the reported F1 score?”, the application might retrieve a child chunk from the results section that surfaces the parent that also spans the methodology and discussion sections. This approach would increase the chance of citing adjacent but irrelevant passages.

options.text: Configure the knowledge base to use semantic chunking. Use a buffer size of 1 and a breakpoint percentile threshold of 85% to determine chunk boundaries based on content meaning.
options.rationale: Semantic chunking groups sentences by meaning similarity and only inserts a split when there is a real topical shift. The buffer keeps each sentence with its immediate neighbors, so references to relevant topics still have their local context inside the same chunk. A buffer size of 1 embeds each sentence with its immediate neighbors, which preserves local flow. A breakpointPercentile setting of 85 would split only the least similar 15% of adjacent sentence pairs. This approach produces fewer, more coherent chunks. This is particularly effective when queries cross multiple sections of a document and reduces off-topic citations from adjacent but unrelated passages.

options.text: Configure the knowledge base not to use chunking. Manually split each document into separate files before ingestion. Apply post-processing reranking during retrieval.
options.rationale: A solution that processes 25 million documents without any chunking would be inefficient and create retrieval challenges. This approach would require significant manual pre-processing and would likely result in chunks that either contain too much information or break semantic relationships. Post-processing reranking could help but would not solve the fundamental issue of maintaining semantic context during the initial retrieval.

options.text: Configure the knowledge base to use fixed-size chunking. Set a 300-token maximum chunk size and a 10% overlap between chunks. Use an appropriate Amazon Bedrock embedding model.
options.rationale: An approach that uses fixed-size chunking with minimal overlap would often break semantic boundaries, which would not address the problem of inconsistent responses that reference irrelevant document sections. This approach maintains a fixed token size regardless of the content's natural semantic divisions and does not maintain semantic context across related paragraphs.

correct_text: Configure the knowledge base to use semantic chunking. Use a buffer size of 1 and a breakpoint percentile threshold of 85% to determine chunk boundaries based on content meaning.

stem: A company is designing an API for a generative AI (GenAI) application that uses a foundation model (FM) that is hosted on a managed model service. The API must stream responses to reduce latency, enforce token limits to manage compute resource usage, and implement retry logic to handle model timeouts and partial responses. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Integrate an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with an AWS Lambda function to invoke Amazon Bedrock. Use Lambda response streaming to stream responses. Enforce token limits within the Lambda function. Implement retry logic for model timeouts by using Lambda and API Gateway timeout configurations.
options.rationale: An API Gateway HTTP API can use an HTTP proxy integration with a Lambda function URL that is configured to stream responses. This approach enables real-time token-by-token delivery to reduce latency. Token limits can be enforced within the Lambda function before the function invokes Amazon Bedrock. You can also implement retry logic for model timeouts in Lambda. This approach meets all requirements with minimal operational overhead.

options.text: Connect an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API directly to Amazon Bedrock. Simulate streaming by using client-side polling. Enforce token limits on the frontend. Configure retry behavior by using API Gateway integration settings.
options.rationale: Client-side polling does not meet the requirement to stream responses because it introduces latency and requires repeated requests instead of receiving tokens in real time. A solution that enforces token limits on the frontend would be operationally inefficient and would not manage compute resource usage at the model invocation layer. API Gateway integration settings would provide limited retry control compared to a solution that uses custom retry logic in Lambda.

options.text: Connect an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to an Amazon ECS service that hosts a containerized inference server. Stream responses by using the WebSocket protocol. Enforce token limits within Amazon ECS. Handle model timeouts by using ECS task lifecycle hooks and restart policies.
options.rationale: A solution that uses an API Gateway WebSocket API and Amazon ECS would require significant operational overhead because it requires management of containerized infrastructure, WebSocket connections, scaling, and task lifecycle behavior. ECS task restart policies and lifecycle hooks operate at the container or task level, not at the request level. This approach could not properly handle model timeouts or partial responses for individual inference calls.

options.text: Integrate an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that invokes Amazon Bedrock. Use Lambda response streaming to stream responses. Enforce token limits within the Lambda function. Implement retry logic by using Lambda and API Gateway timeout configurations.
options.rationale: API Gateway REST APIs do not support Lambda response streaming. This approach would not provide real-time token-level delivery to the client. Lambda and Amazon Bedrock support streaming, but the REST API integration model would not stream responses to reduce latency.

correct_text: Integrate an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with an AWS Lambda function to invoke Amazon Bedrock. Use Lambda response streaming to stream responses. Enforce token limits within the Lambda function. Implement retry logic for model timeouts by using Lambda and API Gateway timeout configurations.

stem: A company updates an Amazon Bedrock based assistant during each development sprint. The company needs an automated deployment validation system. The system must perform prerelease validation and control releases automatically. The system must continuously monitor post-deployment. The system must include alarm capabilities and an automatic rollback functionality. The system must replay synthetic user workflows for key intents. The system must conduct AI-specific evaluations against the production baseline. For example, the evaluations must include hallucination rate and semantic drift analysis. The system must perform automated consistency checks by using a reference prompt set. The company will use an AWS CodePipeline pre-deploy stage that calls an AWS Step Functions workflow to orchestrate the validation checks. Which Step Functions workflow configuration will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries and consistency checks only. Enforce automatic rollback on failures. Schedule hourly runs without model evaluations.
options.rationale: This approach runs hourly consistency checks only without Amazon Bedrock model evaluations, which are required to conduct AI-specific evaluations such as hallucination rate and semantic drift analysis against a production baseline.

options.text: Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluations and Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries. Enforce automatic approval on success. Schedule post-deploy runs with alarms and performance metric tracking.
options.rationale: This approach schedules post-deployment runs with alarms and tracks performance metrics. However, this approach lacks embedding-based consistency checks that compare outputs against reference prompts to detect semantic drift and output quality degradation. Performance metrics focus on operational aspects such as latency and throughput and do not validate semantic consistency across deployments.

options.text: Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluations and consistency checks. Enforce manual approval. Schedule weekly runs without alarms.
options.rationale: This solution enforces manual approval instead of the automatic approval or rollback required to control automated releases. Additionally, weekly scheduled runs would not meet the requirement to provide continuous post-deployment monitoring. This approach would not meet the requirements to provide the alarm capabilities and automatic rollback functionality.

options.text: Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluations and Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries. Run embedding-based consistency checks. Enforce automatic approval or rollback. Schedule nightly runs by using CloudWatch alarms.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock model evaluations provide AI-specific assessments, including faithfulness and coherence metrics that can detect hallucination-like issues and semantic inconsistencies against a production baseline. CloudWatch Synthetics canaries replay synthetic user workflows for key intents. This approach performs prerelease validation by using embedding-based consistency checks and a reference prompt set. This approach also enforces automatic approval or rollback to control releases automatically. This solution can schedule nightly post-deployment runs with CloudWatch alarms to provide continuous monitoring and automatic rollback functionality.

correct_text: Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluations and Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries. Run embedding-based consistency checks. Enforce automatic approval or rollback. Schedule nightly runs by using CloudWatch alarms.

stem: A financial services company is developing a customer service AI assistant by using Amazon Bedrock. The AI assistant must not discuss investment advice with users. The AI assistant must block harmful content, mask personally identifiable information (PII), and maintain audit trails for compliance reporting. The AI assistant must apply content filtering to both user inputs and model responses based on content sensitivity. The company requires an Amazon Bedrock guardrail configuration that will effectively enforce policies with minimal false positives. The solution must provide multiple handling strategies for multiple types of sensitive content. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure multiple guardrails by using tiered policies. Create one guardrail and set content filters to high. Configure the guardrail to block PII for public interactions. Configure a second guardrail and set content filters to medium. Configure the second guardrail to mask PII for internal use. Configure multiple topic-specific guardrails to block investment advice and set up contextual grounding checks.
options.rationale: A solution that uses multiple guardrails that each have different policies would create operational complexity and potential inconsistencies in policy enforcement. This approach would require complex application logic to determine which guardrail to apply and could lead to gaps in coverage or conflicting policy applications. This approach would also increase management overhead and make compliance auditing more difficult because policies would be distributed across multiple guardrails rather than centrally managed. Additionally, contextual grounding checks would reduce hallucinations against a source but would not meet the requirement to mask specific topics, PII, and harmful content.

options.text: Configure a single guardrail and set content filters to high for all categories. Set up denied topics for investment advice and include sample phrases to block. Set up sensitive information filters that apply the block action for all PII entities. Apply the guardrail to all model inference calls.
options.rationale: A solution that sets all content filters to high strength and applies the block action to every PII entity would increase the number of false positives. This approach applies only a single handling strategy rather than the multiple handling strategies for different sensitive content types that this scenario requires.

options.text: Create a separate guardrail for each use case. Create one guardrail that applies a harmful content filter. Create a guardrail to apply topic filters for investment advice. Create a guardrail to apply sensitive information filters to block PII. Use AWS Step Functions to chain the guardrails together sequentially. Use conditional logic based on content classification.
options.rationale: A solution that uses Step Functions to chain separate guardrails sequentially would introduce latency, operational complexity, and potential failure points with no functional benefit over a single guardrail. This approach would require custom orchestration logic in addition to native Amazon Bedrock capabilities, which would increase development and maintenance costs. Sequential processing would introduce the risk that if one guardrail fails, the entire chain could fail. A solution that chains independent guardrails would compound detection errors rather than reduce errors. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can to handle multiple policy types within a single guardrail.

options.text: Configure a guardrail and set content filters to medium for harmful content. Set up denied topics for investment advice and include clear definitions and sample phrases to block. Configure sensitive information filters to mask PII in responses and to block financial information in inputs. Enable both input and output evaluations that use custom blocked messages for audits.
options.rationale: A single guardrail that applies medium-strength content filters balances harmful-content detection against the requirement to minimize the number of false positives. Denied topics that have clear definitions and sample phrases precisely target investment advice restrictions. Sensitive information filters that mask PII in responses and block financial information in inputs deliver the multiple handling strategies that this scenario requires. This solution filters both user prompts and model outputs. Custom blocked messages support the audit and compliance-reporting requirement while maintaining transparency.

correct_text: Configure a guardrail and set content filters to medium for harmful content. Set up denied topics for investment advice and include clear definitions and sample phrases to block. Configure sensitive information filters to mask PII in responses and to block financial information in inputs. Enable both input and output evaluations that use custom blocked messages for audits.

stem: A company is developing an internal generative AI (GenAI) assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize corporate documents for multiple business units. The GenAI assistant must generate responses in a consistent format that includes a document summary, classification of business risks, and terms that are flagged for review. The GenAI assistant must adapt the tone of responses for each user's business unit, such as legal, human resources, or finance. The GenAI assistant must block hate speech, inappropriate topics, and sensitive information such as personal health information. The company needs a solution to centrally manage prompt variants across business units and teams. The company wants to minimize ongoing orchestration efforts and maintenance for post-processing logic. The company also wants to have the ability to adjust content moderation criteria for the GenAI assistant over time. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST maintenance overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define base templates. Enforce business unit-specific tone by using system prompt variables. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to apply audience-based threshold tuning. Manage the guardrails by using an internal administration API.
options.rationale: This approach uses Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to define base templates but enforces department-specific tone by using system prompt variables rather than distinct managed variants. This approach would reduce centralized control and increase the risk of tone or structure drift. Amazon Bedrock guardrails can apply moderation category filters and perform threshold tuning. However, the thresholds are configured for each guardrail instance and cannot be customized for specific audiences or company departments. You must choose a single threshold setting for prompts and responses in a guardrail, and then the guardrail applies universally to all users. To achieve audience-specific threshold behavior, you would need to duplicate guardrail configurations or implement custom routing and orchestration logic. This approach would require additional operational complexity.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock with business unit-based instruction injection in API calls. Store response formatting rules in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Step functions to validate responses. Use Amazon Comprehend to apply content filters after the GenAI assistant generates responses.
options.rationale: This approach would achieve structure and tone control, but it would shift formatting logic into Step Functions and DynamoDB. This approach would require additional orchestration and state management overhead. A solution that uses Amazon Comprehend to perform post-generation filtering would add latency and require extra integration points.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock with custom prompt templates that are stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Create one AWS Lambda function to select business unit-specific prompts. Create a second Lambda function to call Amazon Comprehend to filter prohibited content from responses.
options.rationale: This solution uses a decentralized approach that includes DynamoDB and Lambda. This approach would offer flexibility in prompt selection and filtering by using Amazon Comprehend. However, this approach requires ongoing Lambda orchestration and custom filtering logic. This approach would require more ongoing maintenance and be harder to scale than an approach that uses Amazon Bedrock guardrails.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to configure reusable templates and business unit-specific prompt variants. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails that have category filters and sensitive term lists to block prohibited content.
options.rationale: This approach uses Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to configure centralized, reusable templates that have department-specific variants. This approach ensures that responses always follow a consistent structure, including the summary, risk classification, and flagged terms, without requiring external orchestration logic. Prompt Management gives you the ability to centrally manage prompts to achieve tone and terminology variations for each department in one location. Amazon Bedrock guardrails apply built-in category filters and sensitive term lists to automatically block prohibited content. Guardrails can support iterative updates to categories, term lists, and thresholds without the need to redeploy application code.

correct_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to configure reusable templates and business unit-specific prompt variants. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails that have category filters and sensitive term lists to block prohibited content.

stem: A company used Amazon Bedrock to build a customer support AI assistant. The AI assistant handles approximately 100 requests every second through an Amazon API Gateway API. API Gateway proxies requests to an AWS Lambda function that makes requests to an Amazon Bedrock foundation model (FM) and Amazon DynamoDB tables. The AI assistant is becoming increasingly expensive because customers often send long conversational histories. Many messages repeat the same information or contain low-value details. Token usage has steadily risen, leading to inconsistent latency and unnecessary costs. The company must reduce input token volume without degrading answer quality and without major changes to the existing architecture. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure a new Lambda function to prune repeated or low-value content, summarize long histories by using a small embedding model, and to set maximum input and output token limits in the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API request.
options.rationale: A Lambda function can pre-process conversational histories before sending them to Amazon Bedrock by pruning redundant or low-value content, summarizing long histories by calling a smaller FM to condense context while preserving key information, and setting token limits in requests to the InvokeModel API. This approach directly reduces input token volume, preserves answer quality through summarization, and integrates with the existing architecture.

options.text: For each customer interaction, store the complete conversation history in a DynamoDB table. Send the full history to the FM with every request.
options.rationale: A solution that stores and then sends the complete conversation history for every customer interaction would not meet the requirement to reduce input token volume. This approach would significantly increase token usage, costs, and latency.

options.text: Index all conversations in Amazon OpenSearch Service so the FM can search across the full conversational context before it generates each response.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service provides search and retrieval capabilities but does not reduce token usage. A solution that indexes all conversations in OpenSearch Service and searches across the full context before generating each response would increase system complexity, increase costs, and require the FM to process retrieved content as additional input tokens.

options.text: Replace the current FM with a higher-reasoning model family that supports a larger context window.
options.rationale: A solution that switches to a higher-reasoning model family that has a larger context window would increase the number of tokens the model can accept. However, this approach would not reduce input token volume as required to address rising costs and latency. This approach also requires significant changes to existing architecture.

correct_text: Configure a new Lambda function to prune repeated or low-value content, summarize long histories by using a small embedding model, and to set maximum input and output token limits in the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API request.

stem: A research company is developing a GenAI system to produce summaries of technical documents. The company must catalog all data sources in a central location. The company needs a solution that can automatically discover and update data sources. The solution must tag each generated summary with citations as metadata that users can query. The solution must retain tamper-evident, immutable audit logs for every model invocation and store I/O records. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to identify data sources in the documents. Store generated summaries in Amazon S3 and enable S3 Object Lock. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to generate reports about application throughput. Do not include logs for each invocation.
options.rationale: Amazon Comprehend can extract insights from documents but does not provide a central data catalog. This solution does not meet the requirement to automatically discover and update data sources in a central location. Additionally, CloudWatch metrics provide aggregated statistics rather than the detailed input and output logs for each invocation that are required.

options.text: Use AWS AppConfig feature flags to implement data versioning. Restrict access to the model by using IAM condition keys. Maintain a versioned mapping file of source-to-output relationships in Amazon S3.
options.rationale: AWS AppConfig feature flags are designed to manage application configuration and rollout control, not to catalog data sources or maintain a central, automatically updated data catalog. This solution lacks a central catalog that automatically discovers and updates data sources. Additionally, a versioned mapping file in Amazon S3 would not capture audit logs for each invocation with tamper-evident immutability for every model invocation.

options.text: Store application outputs in Amazon DynamoDB. Apply item-level tags that include source attribution. Write application events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use IAM roles to provide audit traceability.
options.rationale: DynamoDB supports resource-level tags for tables and global secondary indexes. DynamoDB does not support item-level tags, so this solution cannot tag each generated summary with citations as metadata. CloudWatch Logs stores records but does not inherently provide the tamper-evident immutability required for the audit trail. IAM roles control access but do not provide immutable audit logs.

options.text: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog with crawlers to maintain data sources. Store generated summaries in Amazon S3. Write object tags that include a source ID. Store Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs in Amazon S3. Enable S3 Object Lock on the S3 bucket that stores invocation logs. Use AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation to provide tamper-evident immutability.
options.rationale: Glue Data Catalog with crawlers provides a central catalog that automatically discovers and updates data sources. S3 object tags can store object metadata for each object, including source IDs for citations that users can query. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging captures invocation I/O and metadata for each invocation. A solution that stores these logs in Amazon S3 with Object Lock enabled provides immutable retention. CloudTrail can record all Amazon Bedrock API activity with log file integrity validation enabled, which would provide a tamper-evident audit trail for every model invocation.

correct_text: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog with crawlers to maintain data sources. Store generated summaries in Amazon S3. Write object tags that include a source ID. Store Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs in Amazon S3. Enable S3 Object Lock on the S3 bucket that stores invocation logs. Use AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation to provide tamper-evident immutability.

stem: A healthcare company has a mobile app that patients use to check medical symptoms. The app calls an existing Amazon API Gateway REST API that invokes an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function sends user prompts to a foundation model (FM) by using Amazon Bedrock. The company is concerned that patients might send harmful or adversarial prompts and that the model might return hallucinated medical advice or harmful content. The company wants to implement defense-in-depth safety controls for both inputs and outputs. The company wants to use existing integrations with API Gateway and Lambda. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST changes to the app?

options.text: Enable AWS WAF on the API Gateway endpoint. Configure a basic rule set to block specific keywords related to sensitive topics and violence. Allow API Gateway to proxy all other requests directly to the Amazon Bedrock FM. Disable existing Lambda logic.
options.rationale: AWS WAF keyword-based blocking cannot detect nuanced adversarial prompts or hallucinated medical content. A solution that disables existing Lambda logic would not meet the requirement to use existing integrations. This approach would not provide the pre-processing or post-processing validation needed to achieve defense-in-depth. This solution lacks grounding on approved medical content and model-level guardrails.

options.text: Configure Amazon Comprehend to detect personally identifiable information (PII) and sentiment before the app sends prompts to the API. Allow the FM to respond directly through Amazon Bedrock without guardrails. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to manually review a sample of responses for harmful content.
options.rationale: Amazon Comprehend can detect PII and identify sentiment but does not address prompt injection attacks or adversarial inputs. A solution that allows the FM to respond without guardrails would fail to implement model-level safety controls. A solution that implements manual reviews in CloudWatch Logs would not provide real-time protection against harmful outputs or hallucinations.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to block harmful content. Attach the guardrails only to the FM outputs. Allow all user prompts to pass directly to the FM. Use Amazon S3 to store the prompts and completions so a compliance team can review them offline.
options.rationale: A solution that applies guardrails only to outputs would leave the FM exposed to adversarial inputs and prompt injection attack, which would not meet the requirement to provide defense-in-depth safety controls on both inputs and outputs. A solution that relies on offline reviews in Amazon S3 would not provide real-time protection or accuracy verification. This approach lacks pre-processing filters, grounding on approved content, and post-processing validation.

options.text: Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow that invokes a Lambda function to perform input sanitization and prompt injection checks. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter unsafe prompts and responses. Configure the FM to use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that contains approved medical content. Use a post-processing Lambda step to validate responses and to return an error through API Gateway if the response is unsafe or ungrounded.
options.rationale: Step Functions orchestrates multi-layer processing workflows, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards to detect and filter harmful content in both prompts and responses. This solution implements defense-in-depth by combining pre-processing Lambda sanitization, guardrails that apply model-level filtering, knowledge bases to ground responses in approved medical content reducing hallucinations, and post-processing Lambda validation that integrates with API Gateway to return safe responses. This approach reuses the existing API Gateway and Lambda pattern and requires minimal changes to the app.

correct_text: Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow that invokes a Lambda function to perform input sanitization and prompt injection checks. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter unsafe prompts and responses. Configure the FM to use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that contains approved medical content. Use a post-processing Lambda step to validate responses and to return an error through API Gateway if the response is unsafe or ungrounded.

stem: A company is designing a GenAI solution to help children between the ages of 8 and 14 understand world history. The system must support concurrent use for up to 30 children in a classroom and provide responses in less than 1 second. The company is using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Nova Pro with a knowledge base that contains history textbooks that are written for students between the ages of 6 and 21. The company uses an Amazon Bedrock flow to ensure that the solution uses the knowledge base to generate every response. The company sets the prompt response temperature to 0.7. Early testing of the solution results in some responses that are historically inaccurate, violent, and not appropriate for children. A GenAI developer must prevent the solution from responding to prompts inaccurately and inappropriately. Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Increase the inference temperature in the flow. Add a node to the flow after the initial response that calls the Amazon Nova model to remove any violence from the response. Return the result of the model call.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Flows links prompts, FMs, and AWS services to create end-to-end workflows. However, a solution that increases the inference temperature would allow more random and lower-probability token selections, which will reduce determinism and worsen rather than resolve the historical inaccuracy issue. Additionally, a post-processing node to filter violence would increase latency.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) with a custom output that removes all violent content from the knowledge base. Increase the inference temperature in the flow.
options.rationale: BDA transforms unstructured data into meaningful insights by extracting information from documents, images, video, and audio. However, a solution that uses BDA to remove violent content from the knowledge base could over-filter historical content and increase inaccuracy rather than resolve it. Additionally, an approach that increases the inference temperature would reduce adherence to the knowledge base, which would also worsen rather than resolve inaccuracy.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails for the model responses by using content filters. Set the content filter strength high and set the guardrail action to block. Add the guardrail to the flow. Reduce the inference temperature in the flow.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards to detect and filter harmful content in user inputs and model responses, including content filters for categories such as violence. Content filters for model responses that have a high strength and apply block actions ensure that violent content is filtered from responses to children, which meets the requirement to prevent inappropriate responses. This approach adds the guardrail to the flow to apply the guardrail automatically to every invocation. This approach reduces the inference temperature to produce more deterministic responses with higher-probability outputs, which addresses the historical inaccuracy issue.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails for the prompts by using content filters. Set the content filter strength to high and set the guardrail action to block. Add the guardrail to the flow. Reduce the inference temperature in the flow.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock guardrails can filter both prompts and responses. However, a solution that applies guardrails only to prompts would ensure that children cannot send inappropriate requests without meeting the requirement to prevent the model from generating historically inaccurate and violent responses for children.

correct_text: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails for the model responses by using content filters. Set the content filter strength high and set the guardrail action to block. Add the guardrail to the flow. Reduce the inference temperature in the flow.

stem: A financial services company is building an AI-powered research assistant that needs to search through millions of regulatory documents, earnings reports, and marketing documents. The research assistant must handle exact regulatory term matches and conceptual similarity searches. The research assistant must ensure that the most relevant documents are prioritized in the foundation model's (FM's) context window. The company wants the solution to respond to queries in less than 500 ms, achieve 99.9% recall for regulatory terms, and achieve 95% precision for conceptual searches. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Implement hybrid search capabilities in Amazon OpenSearch Service by combining best matching 25 (BM25) keyword matching and vector similarity search. Integrate an Amazon Bedrock Cohere model to score and reorder results. Implement result fusion with weighted scoring.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service hybrid search combines BM25 keyword matching for exact regulatory term matches with vector similarity search for conceptual searches. Amazon Bedrock Cohere reranking models score and optimize result relevance. This solution meets the 99.9% recall requirement by using BM25 exact matching, achieves 95% precision by using vector similarity and reranking, and supports sub-500 ms response times with weighted result fusion to prioritize the most relevant documents in the FM's context window.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to implement keyword-only best matching 25 (BM25) search. Use Amazon Bedrock Cohere embeddings to implement separate vector storage capabilities in Amazon RDS PostgreSQL. Use application-level logic to combine results.
options.rationale: A solution that uses OpenSearch Service to perform keyword search of vectors that are stored in Amazon RDS PostgreSQL will create a distributed architecture that adds network latency and makes it difficult to meet the sub-500 ms response time requirement. An application-level solution to combine results lacks the sophisticated reranking capabilities that Amazon Bedrock Cohere models provide, which can achieve 95% precision for conceptual searches and properly prioritize documents in the FM's context window.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to index documents by using data source connectors. Use Amazon Titan Embeddings to implement semantic search capabilities. Use Amazon Comprehend to extract entities as a post-processing step.
options.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides retrieval capabilities but does not provide the hybrid search capabilities to combine exact keyword matching with vector similarity. A solution that uses Amazon Comprehend to extract entities as a post-processing step would have latency of more than 500 ms and would not provide the reranking capabilities needed to achieve 95% precision for conceptual searches or prioritize documents in the FM's context window.

options.text: Implement Amazon OpenSearch Service vector embeddings and vector similarity search capabilities by using Amazon Titan Embeddings. Directly feed the top-k results to the FM to score and reorder results without additional processing.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service with vector embeddings provides semantic similarity search but does not natively support BM25 keyword matching for exact regulatory term matches. This solution fails to meet the 99.9% recall requirement for regulatory terms because vector-only search cannot guarantee exact term matching. This approach does not provide the reranking capabilities needed to optimize result relevance and achieve 95% precision for conceptual searches.

correct_text: Implement hybrid search capabilities in Amazon OpenSearch Service by combining best matching 25 (BM25) keyword matching and vector similarity search. Integrate an Amazon Bedrock Cohere model to score and reorder results. Implement result fusion with weighted scoring.

stem: A company has a recommendation system. The system's applications run on Amazon EC2 instances. The applications make API calls to Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs) to analyze customer behavior and generate personalized product recommendations. The system is experiencing intermittent issues. Some recommendations do not match customer preferences. The company needs an observability solution to monitor operational metrics and detect patterns of operational performance degradation compared to established baselines. The solution must also generate alerts with correlation data within 10 minutes when FM behavior deviates from expected patterns. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights for the application infrastructure. Set up CloudWatch alarms for latency thresholds. Add custom metrics for token counts by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format. Create CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the data.
options.rationale: This approach monitors latency with alarms and uses the CloudWatch embedded metric format for token counts. However, CloudWatch Container Insights is designed specifically to support containerized applications. This solution lacks the anomaly detection capabilities needed to detect deviations from established baselines.

options.text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights for the application resources. Create custom metrics for recommendation quality, token usage, and response latency by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format with dimensions for request types and user segments. Configure CloudWatch anomaly detection on the model metrics. Establish log pattern analysis by using CloudWatch Logs Insights.
options.rationale: CloudWatch Application Insights can detect anomalies in application metrics and correlate anomalies with logs by using pattern recognition to provide a comprehensive view of operational performance. You can track critical FM interaction patterns and identify which customer groups are receiving inconsistent recommendations by establishing custom metrics for recommendation relevance scores, token usage, and response latency by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format with dimensions for request types and user segments. CloudWatch anomaly detection establishes dynamic baselines for custom metrics and automatically detects deviations in operational patterns, such as unusual latency spikes or token usage anomalies.

options.text: Implement distributed tracing by using Amazon CloudWatch Logs to trace requests through the application components. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to detect error patterns. Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor all API calls to Amazon Bedrock. Create custom dashboards in Amazon Quick Sight.
options.rationale: CloudWatch Logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights provide visibility into request flows and error patterns. CloudTrail logs API calls but cannot monitor operational metrics such as token usage and latency. Quick Sight is a business intelligence service that is not designed to provide real-time operational monitoring. This solution lacks the anomaly detection capabilities needed to detect deviations from established baselines.

options.text: Use Amazon OpenSearch Service with the Observability plugin. Ingest model metrics and logs by using Amazon Kinesis. Create custom Piped Processing Language (PPL) queries to analyze model behavior patterns. Establish operational dashboards to visualize anomalies in real time.
options.rationale: OpenSearch Service can visualize logs and metrics by using the Observability plugin. However, this solution requires building and maintaining a complex data pipeline in Kinesis. This approach is more complex to implement and maintain than a solution that uses native CloudWatch services. PPL queries add unnecessary complexity compared to built-in CloudWatch anomaly detection capabilities.

correct_text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights for the application resources. Create custom metrics for recommendation quality, token usage, and response latency by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format with dimensions for request types and user segments. Configure CloudWatch anomaly detection on the model metrics. Establish log pattern analysis by using CloudWatch Logs Insights.

stem: A legal research company has a RAG application that uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. The application stores 768-dimensional vector embeddings for 15 million legal documents, including statutes, court rulings, and case summaries. The company's current chunking strategy segments text into fixed-length blocks of 500 tokens. The current chunking strategy often splits contextually linked information such as legal arguments, court opinions, or statute references across separate chunks. Researchers report that generated outputs frequently omit key context or cite outdated legal information. Recent application logs show a 40% increase in response times. The p95 latency metric exceeds 2 seconds. The company expects storage needs for the application to grow from 90 GB to 360 GB within a year. The company needs a solution to improve retrieval relevance and system performance at scale. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Replace dynamic retrieval with static, pre-written summaries that are stored in Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the summaries to reduce compute demand and improve predictability.
